linguistic_propositions.proposition: In Form I, a first-position weak consonant is absent from the imperfect stem when that stem carries kasra on the middle radical.
The deletion is motivated by the phonetic heaviness of a prefix vowel followed by that weak consonant.
Members whose imperfect carries fatha on the middle radical keep the first-position weak consonant.
The lesson's own list of fatha-imperfect members includes a high-frequency verb that deletes the consonant anyway, and the conflict is acknowledged but left unexplained.
Because the first-position consonant is already gone, the second-person imperative of Form I is a bare two-consonant syllable with no prosthetic hamza.
The stated imperative derivation adds a prosthetic hamza to that shortened stem, which contradicts the imperative forms the same section then tabulates.
Deletion is confined to Form I; the derived forms keep the first-position weak consonant in every stem.
Under Form VIII the first-position weak consonant merges with the infixed ت, yielding a geminate ت.
ي-initial members lose the root ي in the imperfect when it would stand directly after the ي prefix.
The class name is explained as deriving from the Form VIII merger.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The final weak radical surfaces as a long alif in the bare third-person past cells of both subtypes.
The underlying final consonant reappears whenever a consonant-initial person suffix follows.
The stated motivation, that the long alif appears only where the weak letter would have carried a short vowel, is a derivational account rather than a surface observation.
The two subtypes are distinguished in the imperfect by the vowel preceding the final radical: damma for one, kasra for the other.
The jussive of this class is exponed by deleting the final weak consonant while the preceding vowel remains, so mood is marked by absence.
The subjunctive keeps the final weak consonant and adds fatha to it.
The lesson concedes unspecified classical variation in the subjunctive of the ي subtype without naming the condition or the source.
Several imperfect cells of this class are homographic across person and gender, and the paradigm tables present them without flagging the collision.
A final ي is replaced by و before the masculine plural past suffix.
The vowel carried by the prosthetic hamza of the imperative tracks the subtype vowel of the imperfect.
The deletion rule as stated covers the singular cells; the plural and dual jussive cells are exponed by suffix loss instead, which the lesson shows in a paradigm without stating.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The identical second and third radicals merge into a single geminate consonant wherever the following material does not force them apart.
They separate before a consonant-initial person suffix.
The condition is phonotactic: a geminate may not stand immediately before a vowelless consonant.
In the imperfect only the feminine plural cells separate, because only their suffix is consonant-initial.
Both a merged jussive ending in fatha and a separated jussive ending in sukun are grammatical for the same cell.
The lesson presents exactly two licensed jussive shapes; grammars additionally license a merged variant ending in kasra, which is not mentioned.
The merged jussive is characterised as belonging to classical prose and the separated one to Quranic and poetic usage; this register split is asserted without evidence or attribution.
The imperfect middle vowel is unpredictable and belongs to the lexical entry.
One heading labels the fatha-imperfect subpattern with the template name of the kasra-imperfect subpattern; the body of the lesson uses the correct label.
The imperative of this class takes no prosthetic hamza because the merged stem opens with a vowelled consonant.
A merged form ending in damma after a jussive operator is an indicative rather than a licensed jussive variant.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Hamza is a root consonant, and verbs containing it form a class separate from the weak classes.
The contrast is drawn against roots said to contain ا as a weak radical alongside و and ي.
Carrier selection follows a precedence in which kasra outranks damma, which outranks fatha, with a bare hamza after a vowelless letter.
The environments are tabulated as holding after a given vowel, while the closing summary states the same rule bidirectionally; the two statements of one rule do not agree.
One cited illustration of a damma-seated hamza is a form outside ordinary usage for that verb.
Three initial-hamza verbs lose the hamza in the imperative, because the derivation would otherwise stack a prosthetic hamza on a root hamza.
One medial-hamza verb loses its hamza throughout the imperfect, jussive and imperative, and is presented as a stored item rather than a rule output.
In the first-person singular imperfect of an initial-hamza verb, the prefix hamza and the root hamza contract into a long alif.
Carrier selection is presented as fully determined by the adjacent vowels, whereas word-final position and editorial orthographic convention also condition the written carrier.
Membership in a hamza subclass is orthogonal to membership in a weak class, so the two labels must not be substituted for one another.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The separated subtype behaves as first-radical-weak at the front of the stem and as final-radical-weak at its end, within a single word.
The derivation offered for the shortened imperfect and jussive, running from a long underlying form through assimilation to deletion, is a rule-ordering account rather than a surface observation.
The jussive of the separated subtype leaves a single visible root consonant.
The imperative of the separated subtype is a single consonant with kasra and takes no prosthetic hamza.
The adjacent subtype is characterised as having و in second position and ي in third; this excludes attested members with other weak-letter combinations in those positions.
The adjacent subtype's imperfect is described as a hollow-plus-defective combination, although its middle weak letter is a vowelless consonant rather than the long vowel of a hollow stem.
In both subtypes the past behaves like the simple final-weak class, including restoration before consonant-initial suffixes and the plural-suffix shift.
The jussive of the adjacent subtype deletes only the final radical and keeps the middle one.
Indefinite active participles of both subtypes lose the final radical and close on tanwin with kasra.
The past tense of the separated subtype shows no deletion of the first radical, so the deletion of the previous lesson is confined to the imperfect stem.
This class is described as the morphologically most complex set of Form I verbs.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The passive is formed by replacing a stem's internal vowels; no consonant is added or removed.
Because the imperfect passive melody fixes fatha on the middle radical, the lexically stored active imperfect vowel is not recoverable from a passive form.
Medial-weak stems take kasra plus a long ي in the past passive and a long alif in the imperfect passive.
The three motivations listed for using the passive are pragmatic and discourse-level rather than grammatical conditions on its formation.
The statement of the third-radical vowel in the past passive is left loose and does not separate the bare cell from suffixed cells.
Passive melodies for the final-weak, doubly weak and geminate classes taught earlier in this same module are not stated anywhere in the lesson.
The passive paradigm includes first- and second-person cells whose morphology is regular even though their use is restricted.
In the passive the original direct object becomes the grammatical subject and takes nominative marking.
The consonant skeleton of an active and a passive Form I verb is identical, so in unvocalised text voice is not readable from the letters alone; the lesson teaches the melodies without noting this.
Derived-form passives are stated for three forms only, and the pattern is left to be generalised by the learner to the rest of the series.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A passive verb still requires a subject, and the promoted patient fills that position with nominative marking.
Agreement of a passive verb with its deputy agent follows the same gender and number rules as agreement with an agent, including feminine singular agreement for non-human plurals.
The role can be filled by an interpreted verbal-noun clause, or by a prepositional phrase or adverbial when the verb has no patient to promote.
When a prepositional phrase or adverbial fills the position, its nominative status is positional and is not shown on the phrase itself; the lesson tabulates such cases without saying so.
With a covert pronoun subject the role has no surface exponent and must be inferred from context.
The agent of a passive verb may be expressed by a phrase headed by بـ or by another preposition, on the model of an English by-phrase.
Reading every prepositional phrase after a passive verb as an agent phrase would misanalyse the instrumental, causal and circumstantial uses of the same prepositions, which are far more frequent.
The lesson's own error section reinforces the agent-phrase reading by labelling a prepositional phrase as a mentioned agent.
The motivations given for using the passive are pragmatic rather than structural.
A first-person suffix on a passive verb is analysed as itself filling the deputy-agent role.
The construction is presented as a mechanical transformation of an active sentence, which is a teaching device rather than a claim about how the two are related.

verb-subject agreement including the non-human plural rule

new_knowledge: a named syntactic role defined by position rather than by semantics
argument promotion as a syntactic operation with case consequences
a subject position that may be filled by a non-nominal constituent
passives of verbs that never had a direct object

sarf_relevance: medium + the role can only be identified once the passive melody of the previous lesson has been read off the verb
nahw_relevance: high + it is a governance and case-assignment topic covering argument promotion, agreement, and positional case for non-nominal fillers
tutor_drill_relevance: strong for conversion drills and for role-identification drills over running text; drills must include intransitive passives with phrasal fillers and covert-pronoun cases, and must not reward reading a prepositional phrase as an agent
rich_hover_relevance: high: a hover on a nominative noun after a verb should say whether it is an agent or a deputy agent and on what evidence, and should not label a following prepositional phrase as an agent
corpus_pvn_relevance: particle entries (p) matter most here, because the lesson's weakest claim concerns a preposition being read as an agent marker and those prepositions are extremely frequent; verb entries (v) need voice recorded; noun entries (n) are affected only through case annotation
required_evidence: per occurrence: the vocalisation or other evidence establishing that the verb is passive, the case of the candidate nominal, the agreement facts, and, before any agent reading of a prepositional phrase, positive evidence that the phrase is not instrumental, causal or circumstantial
uncertainty_flags: the agent-by-preposition construction as presented is not a standard licence of the passive and its illustrations should be treated as candidate material pending review
phrasal fillers are labelled nominative without distinguishing positional from marked case
the active-to-passive transformation is presented as a derivational fact rather than as a teaching device
the lesson is a syntax lesson closing a module whose stated subject is weak and geminate conjugation, so its placement in the sequence is not motivated by the module title

unit_mapping.equivalence_basis: Not redundant. u-n01 covers case exponence and u-n03 covers governance, but neither carries argument promotion under passivisation; u-n08 gains a concrete deleted-constituent case (the absent agent) and u-n09 gains a positional-nominative case (a prepositional phrase or adverbial occupying a subject position); u-n10 gains a referent-resolution case for covert pronoun fillers. The one genuinely new decision procedure, telling an agent from a deputy agent on a bare nominative, is proposed as a unit below.

proposed_new_units.summary: given a verb and a following nominative nominal, decide whether the nominal is the agent or the deputy agent, listing the evidence each decision requires and marking the cases that are undecidable without vocalisation
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n03 states that a verb governs its subject but does not distinguish the two subject roles, and u-n01 marks nominative case without saying which role earned it; in unvocalised text this discrimination is exactly where a reader silently guesses
